subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
The loan camp at Kheda's panchayat hall ran from ten till four, and by the end sixty-two farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed. Not one had to come back.
On the bus back to the branch, Damini, the branch manager, turned round in her seat. 'Tanvir, that was the smoothest camp we've had in three years. Your checklist at the door saved hours.'
Tanvir smiled and looked out at the cotton fields. 'The sarpanch had told everyone what to bring, ma'am. And you did the planning. Honestly, it was an easy village.'
Damini frowned slightly but let it go.
That night, going over the register, he found he'd written one farmer's survey number with two digits reversed. His stomach dropped. He corrected it, then sat staring at the page. There, he thought. That's the real me. The camp was luck.

qa.q: How many farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed?
qa.a: Sixty-two farmers had their crop-loan forms checked and signed.

qa.q: What does Tanvir's thought 'That's the real me' reveal about how he sees himself?
qa.a: He believes his success was luck and that one small mistake is the true proof he isn't good enough.

qa.q: What could Tanvir try the next time Damini praises his work?
qa.a: He could simply say thank you and write down what he actually did, like the checklist, instead of giving the credit away.

qa.q: How might Damini see Tanvir's answer on the bus?
qa.a: Damini may feel puzzled or a bit frustrated that her honest praise was brushed aside, since she saw his checklist make the difference.

grounding: It shows a young officer crediting luck, the team and an easy village for a success, and treating one small error as proof of not being good enough.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Anders put Hana's packaging design up on the big screen at the Monday meeting in the Copenhagen studio. The client, a small tea company, had approved it on the first round, which Anders said almost never happened.
'Hana did this,' he told the room. 'The fold-out label was her idea.'
People clapped. Hana felt her face go hot. 'It was a simple brief,' she said. 'And Mikkel fixed the typeface for me.'
Mikkel, across the table, looked confused. He had changed one letter spacing.
At lunch, Hana told herself that Anders probably praised everyone like that, that the client just liked green.
On Tuesday, a printer proof came back with one colour slightly off. Nobody else seemed worried; it was a two-minute fix. Hana stayed late anyway, rereading every file, sure that this, finally, was the moment they would see what she really was.

qa.q: Which part of the design did Anders say was Hana's idea?
qa.a: Anders said the fold-out label was her idea.

qa.q: How does Hana feel about the praise in the meeting, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and unsure she deserves it; her face goes hot and she gives the credit to the easy brief and to Mikkel.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Hana handled the small colour error, and what could help?
qa.a: She treated a two-minute fix as proof she was a fraud; checking the facts, such as the first-round approval, could balance that fear.

qa.q: How does Mikkel see the credit Hana gave him?
qa.a: Mikkel is confused, because he knows he only changed one letter spacing and the design was really hers.

grounding: It shows a young designer crediting an easy brief and a colleague for her success, dismissing praise, and treating one small error as proof.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Hi Seema,
You asked about the client pitch. Well, we won it. The partner took the whole team to dinner and made a speech about my deck, which was very embarrassing.
Honestly, it was mostly luck. The client had already half-decided, and Karan did all the numbers. I just made the slides look nice. Anyone would have got the same result. When the partner said I have "a real gift for storytelling", I smiled and thought, he'll figure out soon that he's wrong about that.
Then on Monday I sent a report with a typo in the client's name. One letter. I've felt sick about it for three days. That's the real me, I think. The dinner was a fluke; the typo is the truth.
Tell me about your new flat? I need distracting.
Love,
Elizabeth

qa.q: What mistake did Elizabeth make on Monday?
qa.a: A typo in the client's name, one letter.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth mean by 'the typo is the truth'?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels anxious and ashamed, treating one small error as proof of being a fraud while dismissing the win as a fluke.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth try to see the win more fairly?
qa.a: List what was actually done for the pitch, the deck and the storytelling the partner praised, and set it beside a one-letter typo.

qa.q: How might Seema feel reading this email?
qa.a: Seema may feel worried and a little frustrated, seeing Elizabeth brush off a real success and dwell on a tiny mistake.

grounding: A young professional credits a won pitch to luck and a teammate, files praise as a mistake and treats one typo as proof.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Bidisha, stop, you're making it bigger than it was. Yes, the release went fine. Yes, my fix stopped the crash that had been bugging the team for a month. But honestly, they gave me the easy ticket. Anyone would have found it once they looked at the logs.
And the tech lead thanking me in the all-hands? That's just him being nice to the new person. Everyone gets that in their first months. I'm Dolma, remember, the one who still looks up basic commands every single day.
You know what I keep replaying? The code review last week where I named a variable badly and someone left a comment. That's the stuff that shows who I really am. The thank-you is a mistake he'll correct soon enough.
Don't give me that face. I'm just being realistic. Anyway, your turn. How was your week?

qa.q: How long had the crash been bothering the team?
qa.a: For a month.

qa.q: What is Dolma feeling when replaying the code review comment?
qa.a: Dolma feels anxious and ashamed, treating one small comment as proof of not belonging while dismissing the praise.

qa.q: What would help Dolma see this success honestly?
qa.a: Asking the tech lead what exactly the fix did well, and noting that the crash took the team a month to solve, would test the 'easy ticket' story.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see Dolma's explanation?
qa.a: Bidisha likely feels puzzled and concerned, watching a friend explain away a real success as luck and politeness.

grounding: A young engineer credits a successful fix to an easy assignment, files thanks as politeness and treats a small comment as proof.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Monday. Ayesha's forecast for the festival season came back almost exact, within two per cent of real sales. Irfan, her manager, forwarded it to the whole department with "Brilliant work". Ayesha replied, "Thanks, the data was quite clean this time," and closed the tab.
Wednesday. In the team meeting Irfan asked her to explain her method. She said, "Honestly, I just used the template Ravi made. I got lucky with the season." Ravi looked surprised; he had only shared a blank sheet.
Friday. A small chart in her weekly report had the wrong label on one axis. A colleague pointed it out gently. Ayesha stayed back till eight redoing the whole report, stomach tight, thinking, now they'll see what I really am. She never opened Monday's email again.

qa.q: How close was Ayesha's forecast to real sales?
qa.a: Within two per cent of real sales.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling when she stayed back till eight on Friday?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed, treating one wrong label as proof she was a fraud.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Ayesha on Wednesday?
qa.a: She could explain her real method and accept the credit, instead of handing it to Ravi's template and luck.

qa.q: How might Irfan see Ayesha's replies to his praise?
qa.a: Irfan may feel puzzled or a little frustrated that his sincere praise keeps getting brushed aside.

grounding: Across a week a young analyst credits luck and a colleague for her success while treating one small error as proof she is a fraud.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage: "Kamal, sit. You're making that face again, the one that says 'it was just luck'. I know it well, because I wore it for years. At twenty-four I joined the newspaper in Pune as a junior sub-editor. In my second month I wrote a headline for the flood story that the editor pinned on the notice board. Everyone congratulated me. And what did I say? 'Oh, the story was so strong, anyone could have done it.' When I was moved up to the city page, I told myself they were short of people. But one small spelling mistake in a caption, and I cried in the ladies' room, sure that now they would see the truth about me. Praise went in one ear and out the other. Mistakes, I kept like a diary. Your Irawati aaji took twenty years to learn to keep both."

qa.q: What did young Irawati write that was pinned on the notice board?
qa.a: A headline for the flood story.

qa.q: How did young Irawati feel about the caption mistake?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and frightened, sure that now they would see the truth about her.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have helped young Irawati?
qa.a: Keeping the praise, like the pinned headline and the move to the city page, as carefully as the mistakes, instead of explaining it away.

qa.q: How might the editor have seen young Irawati's work?
qa.a: The editor clearly valued it, pinning the headline and later moving her up, even while she believed it was luck.

grounding: Shows a young worker crediting luck or the story for every success while treating one small error as proof of being found out.
